inputs.label: Watershed impervious cover
inputs.rationale: Impervious cover represents altered infiltration, runoff routing, and hydrologic flashiness.

inputs.label: Watershed agricultural cover
inputs.rationale: Agricultural cover represents a separate soil-disturbance, drainage, and runoff pathway that impervious cover does not capture.

limitations: The worse input governs because hydrologic alteration through one pathway is not offset by low pressure in the other.
Agricultural bands are national screening tiers, not ecological criteria.
A result computed from one input is labeled partial.

Sensitive macroinvertebrate taxa decline well below the 10 percent impervious Good boundary (community thresholds near 0.5 to 2 percent), so a Good rating is not a no-effect finding (King et al. 2011).

breakpoints.description: Lower national screening transition. Watershed wetland extents of 1 to 5 percent are associated with water-quality benefit and about 7 percent with flood attenuation (Mitsch and Gosselink, as reviewed by the Chesapeake Bay Program 2016).
Upper national screening transition, the top of the same reviewed 1 to 5 percent benefit range.

inputs.rationale: Woody wetlands contribute surface storage and hydrologic attenuation.

inputs.label: Herbaceous wetland cover
inputs.rationale: Herbaceous wetlands contribute storage not represented by woody-wetland cover.

limitations: Natural wetland abundance varies substantially among regions.

breakpoints.description: Lower STAF screening transition. It is not a demonstrated ecological threshold.

breakpoints.label: 3 km/km²

inputs.label: Watershed road density
inputs.rationale: Road density is a directional proxy for concentrated runoff sources and hillslope-to-channel connectivity.

limitations: Road density does not count actual outfalls or establish whether runoff is treated.
The 1 km/km² breakpoint is a screening judgment.

USFS watershed-condition guidance classes road density more strictly (good under 1, impaired over 2.4 miles per square mile, about 0.62 and 1.49 km/km²), derived from salmonid watersheds. EASI keeps the NRSA-anchored national screen and discloses the stricter alternative.

breakpoints.description: Onset-of-regulation boundary. Comparative global assessment treats storage above 2 percent of annual flow as regulated (Lehner et al. 2011).
breakpoints.label: 2% DOR

breakpoints.description: Severe-regulation boundary. The free-flowing rivers analysis uses 15 percent as its operational pressure limit, the high end of a published 2 to 15 percent range (Grill et al. 2019). It is not a regulatory standard.
breakpoints.label: 15% DOR

inputs.label: Upstream normalized storage
inputs.rationale: Upstream storage is the regulated volume available to alter the natural flow regime.

inputs.label: Annual runoff
inputs.rationale: Annual runoff converts storage to a dimensionless degree of regulation relative to the river's annual water volume.

limitations: Degree of regulation does not describe operating rules, diversions, seasonality, or dam location on the network.
Missing or non-positive runoff is not converted to zero and leaves the metric unscored.
methods.title: Flow alteration (degree of regulation)

inputs.label: Monthly flow variability
inputs.rationale: Population standard deviation of all twelve mean monthly flows divided by their mean. All months must be finite and the mean must be positive.
inputs.sourceField: NHDPlus V2 EROM QE_01 through QE_12

inputs.label: EROM mean annual flow
inputs.rationale: Mean annual modeled flow provides scale context; it does not determine the rating.

inputs.label: Expected NHD flow regime
inputs.rationale: Flow classification provides context for natural intermittency and does not determine the rating.

limitations: Unvalidated screening proxy for low-flow condition. Agreement with the field wetted-channel measure was weak (0.18).
Monthly climatological variability is not a measurement of daily low flow, baseflow contribution, or wetted connectivity.
NARS-9 curves compare variability with regional reference expectations; lower variability rates better. A national curve is the fallback.
All twelve months are required. Missing months are unknown, not zero. Natural intermittent and ephemeral streams require interpretation.

sourceHierarchy.description: Use all twelve modeled monthly flows; missing or nonpositive-mean flow remains unscored.

inputs.label: Bank-height ratio
inputs.rationale: BHR directly measures the vertical separation between bankfull flow and the low floodplain surface.

limitations: A BHR below 1.0 remains Good but requires geometry verification.

inputs.rationale: ER directly represents lateral floodplain width available relative to the bankfull channel.

limitations: National reference curves group channel slopes below 0.5 percent, from 0.5 to below 2 percent, and at least 2 percent.
An unsplit national reference curve is used when slope is unknown. Naturally confined valleys still require field interpretation.
Entrenchment ratio measures floodplain access; it does not establish channel stability or flood frequency.
methods.title: Floodplain access (entrenchment ratio)

breakpoints.description: Lower screening transition, carried over from the prior exchange-potential index. A screening judgment, not a published threshold.
breakpoints.label: 0.003 m/m

breakpoints.description: Upper screening transition, carried over from the prior exchange-potential index. A screening judgment, not a published threshold.
breakpoints.label: 0.006 m/m

breakpoints.description: Boundary between straight and sinuous planform in common geomorphic classifications. A screening judgment, not a published threshold.

Boundary above which meandering is well expressed in generalized reach geometry and lateral exchange across bends is expected (Boano et al. 2006, Cardenas 2009). A screening judgment, not a published threshold.

inputs.label: Channel slope
inputs.rationale: Slope sets the vertical hydraulic gradient that drives bedform-driven bed exchange, the dominant hyporheic pathway in steeper channels.

inputs.label: Reach sinuosity
inputs.rationale: Sinuosity indicates lateral exchange through meander necks and point bars, the dominant hyporheic pathway in low-gradient meandering channels. Because the better pathway governs, sinuosity understated by generalized reach geometry can only fail to credit lateral exchange, never lower the rating.

limitations: Slope screens vertical bedform-driven exchange and sinuosity screens lateral meander-driven exchange. Bed hydraulic conductivity is a co-dominant control that is unavailable, so steep reaches over bedrock or fine beds can overpredict exchange.
The better pathway governs because vertical and lateral exchange are alternative mechanisms. Either alone indicates exchange potential.

Sinuosity measured over generalized reach geometry understates planform sinuosity. Under the better-pathway rule that bias can only fail to lift a rating, never lower one. The earlier weighted slope and sinuosity composite was retired for exactly that downward bias.
A result computed from one pathway is labeled partial.
The slope and sinuosity bands are screening judgments, not published thresholds.
methods.title: Hyporheic-exchange potential (channel gradient or sinuosity)

BHR retains its 1.3/1.5 bands; ER uses national reference curves by slope class, with an unsplit national fallback when slope is unknown.
Canal/ditch classification and documented field-stage overrides remain decisive. Naturally confined valleys require field interpretation.

inputs.label: Bank-height ratio
inputs.rationale: BHR is an established incision and floodplain-connectivity measure used here only as a susceptibility proxy, not as measured erosion or armoring.

limitations: BHR does not detect existing armoring and does not directly measure erosion rate or eroding-bank extent.
The DEM-derived cross section is a susceptibility screen and may require surveyed geometry.
BHR is reused by floodplain engagement and channel adjustment and is therefore correlated evidence.

sourceHierarchy.description: Complete user observations of both components supersede the proxy.

breakpoints.description: Lower EASI transition for observed erosion extent.

Any observed hard armoring moves the armoring component out of Good.
Half or more of the bank length armored is classified Poor. Armoring of 75% or more is annotated as pervasive.

inputs.label: Eroding bank
inputs.rationale: Percent eroding bank directly records the longitudinal extent of active erosion.

inputs.label: Armored bank
inputs.rationale: Percent armored bank directly records the extent of hard bank protection, which BHR cannot detect.

inputs.label: Annual bank retreat
inputs.rationale: Retreat rate may support interpretation but receives no universal class without a regional reference rate.

limitations: The 5%, 50%, and 60% class limits are transparent EASI screening judgments. The 30% erosion and 75% armoring marks are interpretive annotations.
Annual retreat requires a regional reference rate and is supporting evidence only.

inputs.rationale: K-factor represents inherent soil erodibility, the susceptibility term no other metric screens.

inputs.rationale: Roads are both a sediment source and a hillslope-to-channel connectivity pathway.

limitations: The worse input governs. Source indicators are screened separately and are not summed.
Intrinsic soil erodibility (K-factor) can lower the rating in undisturbed watersheds. It indicates susceptibility rather than an active source.
The road-density bands derive from salmonid watershed criteria applied here nationally.
Agricultural cover and road density are also rated by other metrics and are therefore correlated evidence.
All three inputs are required. Missing inputs are not converted to zero.
